paper_title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock's 4.46$\times$ to 10.87$\times$ with one request, and from 1.94$\times$ to 3.93$\times$ with batching.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Speculative decoding [1, 2] accelerates memory-bound autoregressive (AR) decoding of large language models (LLMs) with lightweight drafter, so one target pass accepts several tokens. AR drafters such as EAGLE-3 [3] draft sequentially, while parallel drafters such as DFlash [4], DFlash2 [5] and DSpark [6] draft block of 8 or 16 tokens per forward pass. However, their released systems (stock) leave much of this potential unrealized. With one request, reading the target weights dominates the per-step latency (Figure 2a), so verifying additional tokens adds little extra latency. Stock still verifies only one drafted chain, ignoring the other candidates that its drafter ranks at each position, which often include the targets next token. Using them would accept about twice as many tokens per step (3.1). With batching, each request adds its own attention, recurrent-state and prefill work, so weight reads no longer dominate the step, and stocks speedup over AR decoding roughly halves (Figure 2b). Existing techniques such as draft trees [710] and batch-aware speculation [1113] are general, but the best choice depends on the deployment. deployment comprises serving regime, drafter, target and GPU platform, and each changes what pays off. The serving regime can turn gain into loss. Checking drafts with low-precision target copy before the exact pass Figure 1: Speedup over AR with one request. SpecPilot more than doubles stocks speedup in each setting. speeds up decoding with one request, but with batching on BF16 Qwen3.8-27B the same idea is 13% slower, because the extra check takes nearly step. The drafter decides how to score draft tree. DSpark conditions each drafted token on the one before it, and tree that ignores this accepts half the tokens of one using it. The target and the GPU decide what each mechanism costs. tree on hybrid Qwen3.8-27B [14] must track every nodes recurrent state (2.3), and the RTX PRO 6000 lacks Hoppers wgmma instructions, so kernels need porting. No universal optimization fits every deployment. Manually optimizing each deployment does not scale, whereas coding agents [15, 16] iterate rapidly. This makes per-deployment optimization natural fit for them, and agentic optimizers such as AlphaEvolve and ADRS already evolve programs against automated evaluators [17, 18]. For lossless speculative decoding, however, building reliable evaluator is difficult for two reasons. First, many gains are only few percent, close to timing noise, and gain measured on development requests may not generalize to unseen ones. Second, an agent rewarded for speed is prone to reward hacking [19, 20], such as adopting faster numerical shortcut that changes outputs without measurable drop in task accuracy (Figure 2c). We present SpecPilot (Figure 3), an autonomous agentic loop that searches for speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. It rests on four ideas. First, cost model compares measured performance with an estimated ceiling to locate where speed is lost. Second, parallel agents explore multiple directions on separate GPUs and integrate the validated pieces, so small gains add up. Third, controller isolated from the agents accepts change only on significant gain confirmed on unseen requests, and token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect lossy changes (3.3). Finally, validated optimizations are distilled into structured memory as replayable code and evidence, for reuse in later rounds and new deployments. The loop developed lossless techniques, each targeting gap the cost model measured (4). Best-first tree verification exploits idle drafter candidates, even on hybrid recurrent targets, and W12, general lossless 12-bit weight format, cuts the weight reads dominating single-request steps. Two-level verification pre-checks drafts at low precision, nearly doubling accepted tokens per exact pass. For batching, three mechanisms spend verify rows where they pay off (4.4). We evaluate SpecPilot on four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stocks 4.46 to 10.87 with one request (Figure 1), and from 1.94 to 3.93 with batching. On H100 with one request, it is 1.84 faster than DDTree [10]. 2 Figure 2: (a) Single-request step time split into target weights and the rest, at peak bandwidth and as measured after the first optimization round. Reading the weights dominates the step. (b) Stock speedup over AR falls as the batch size grows, for Qwen3.8-27B in FP8 and Qwen3.5-4B in BF16. (c) Task accuracy change against stock, with 95% CIs, for lossless system and faulty one with an injected logit bias. All four intervals include zero, so accuracy cannot flag the faulty systems. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions: Autonomous Optimization Loop: We design SpecPilot, ceiling-guided agentic framework that tailors speculative decoding to each deployment and transfers validated optimizations across hardware and models via structured memory. To prevent reward hacking, we introduce token forcing, stock-calibrated test that detects output divergences task accuracy misses. Discovered Lossless Algorithms: SpecPilot discovered W12, general lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three mechanisms for batching. Cross-Regime Bottleneck Analysis: We show how ceiling-guided discovery adapts to both memory-bandwidth and per-row compute bottlenecks, and why the same mechanism can accelerate one request but slow decoding with batching on the same GPU.

2.1 Speculative Decoding
In speculative decoding [1, 2], a drafter proposes m tokens ˆx1..m after the prefix x<t, and the
target model verifies them in one forward pass, one row per token. Greedy decoding accepts
the longest prefix with ˆxi = arg max p(· | x<t, ˆx<i) and adds the target’s argmax as a bonus,
accepting τ ∈ [1, m + 1] tokens.

Its output is then the targets greedy decode up to floating-point reduction order, such as GEMM tiling or tree attention, which can change token only at logit near-tie. Stock already differs from AR in this way. At each first divergence, the two tokens log-probabilities differ by at most 0.232 nats (3.3). low-precision verify pass, by contrast, can change tokens even far from near-ties. Each round distills its mechanisms into memory entries, which carry to later rounds and new deployments.

sections.content: SpecPilot operates in rounds (Figure 3). round measures where the current system loses speed (Phase 0), lets agents build and time changes (Phases 13) and ends with sealed final on unseen requests (Phase 4). sections.title:
3.2 Agents and Phases
SpecPilot separates the agents that modify the system from the controller that measures it
(Figure 3). A master agent plans directions, one idea per GPU, each with an estimated headroom
(expected gain). A sub-agent implements each direction as patches, code changes behind options
whose defaults reproduce stock. A patch must pass correctness checks and token forcing (§3.3) on
sections.content: 5 Figure 4: Token forcing on lossless and faulty systems in sealed finals. Bars give the mismatch rate with 95% CIs, and dashed lines the rate-rule limit. Above the bars are the verdict and the count of large-margin events. Faulty systems add logit bias of 2 to every 7th vocabulary id after 2048 tokens. development requests, which agents see. The controller, scripts that agents call but cannot modify, times it against the current best in paired runs, where both systems serve the same requests on two GPUs, swapping GPUs between runs. It promotes the patch only if its gains 95% lower bound exceeds 1% plus twice the stock-versus-stock noise (< 0.1% for one request on H100), or 3% if its outputs diverge from the current bests. Phase 1: Exploration. The master starts from Phase 0s cost model and proposes directions aimed at its largest factors. single direction can stall on an idea that does not pay off, so the master explores the most promising few at once. sub-agent first checks the headroom with the cheapest evidence, such as exact replay, microbenchmark or timing run on one GPU. It builds new algorithm only if the headroom, net of runtime overhead, is at least 3%. It closes direction only after measuring the implemented mechanism, unless that would take over 10 GPU-minutes. Phases 23: Integration and kernel tuning. Many patches gain too little to promote alone, but enough together. An integration sub-agent stacks them on the current best and times the stack under the same rule. kernel sub-agent profiles it and tunes kernels furthest from byte floors. Phase 4: Sealed final. Each round ends with sealed final, which times the system against stock on unseen requests and reruns token forcing on its outputs and on longer outputs of up to 4096 tokens. final that fails either check is rejected. worked example. In round two, step cost led (6.1), so the master opened direction cutting weight bytes (W12, Figure 5). Byte arithmetic put its headroom at 25% of the 15.30 ms weight read, and microbenchmark closed denser 11-bit variant that decoded 3 slower. The first patch was promoted at 1.076 in paired runs and revised kernel gave 1.063. The DSpark, RTX PRO 6000 and Muse-Glimmer deployments reused W12 from memory (5.3).

3.3 Token Forcing
Losslessness holds by construction (§4). Token forcing tests the implementation against stock
for bugs and reward hacking. A teacher-forced scorer feeds the system’s outputs back through
the target on the stock engine with an FP32 LM head. A token is a mismatch if it differs from the
scorer’s argmax, and its margin is the log-probability gap to that argmax. Stock mismatches on
0.72% of tokens, almost all near-ties from kernel rounding. Phase 0 sets the near-tie threshold δ
by rounding up the largest margin at stock’s first departures from AR to a multiple of 1/8.

sections.title: 4 Discovered Lossless Algorithms
sections.content: We describe each mechanism and why it is lossless.

sections.title:
4.1 W12: A Lossless 12-bit Weight Format
W12 reduces the step cost relative to AR decoding by reading fewer bytes per weight while
keeping every bit exact. Most BF16 weights in an output channel span only a few binades (powers
of two). For each channel n, W12 selects the 16-binade window [En − 15, En] that covers the most
weights. Each weight with in-window exponent e is stored as its sign bit, a 4-bit exponent offset
e − (En − 15), and its seven mantissa bits, for a total of 12 bits (Figure 5a). Weights outside the
window, zeros and denormals become escapes, which a sparse per-channel list restores exactly.
W12 averages only 12.01–12.02 bits per weight on eight dense models and shrinks Qwen3.8-27B’s

Each 12 KB record covers 12864 weight tile. An INT8 copy with per-row CauchySchwarz error bound discards every token that provably cannot be the argmax, and the survivors are rescored exactly. When too many survive, the full head runs instead. The argmax thus never changes. This reduces LM head latency from 878 to 482 µs, outperforming W12. On the RTX PRO 6000, the certified head is slower than BF16 (2598 vs. 1750 µs), so W12 converts the LM head there.

4.2 Tree Verification for Hybrid Targets
Round one built best-first trees (Figure 6) on the DFlash2 lattice, scoring each edge by log softmax
of selector scores given its parent, not by DDTree’s marginal scores [10]. The drafter runs 16
positions, twice its trained block size, and the tree verifies N=32 nodes up to depth 15, more
than the drafted positions (a wide tree).
sections.content: Recurrent state without snapshots. SpecPilot recomputes the recurrent state along each root path instead of storing it per node. path verify kernel walks each path from the committed state, and commit kernel replays the accepted path into all 48 GDN layers, matching the stock kernel bit for bit on chains. The faster WY verify kernel, following TreeWY [22], turns the chain of rank-one updates in Eq. (2) into matrix products, solving all paths at once on tensor cores. It splits the FP32 state into three BF16 parts that represent all 24 significand bits exactly, accumulates tensor-core products in FP32, and stays within one BF16 ulp of the path kernels outputs. sections.title:
4.3 Two-Level Verification
Each TLV cycle has two passes (Figure 7). A Q pass over the 8-bit view of W12 checks the draft
tree and returns the path that matches its argmax and a bonus token as a chain C, without
updating the KV cache or the recurrent state. The drafter drafts again from the end of C, and
its best-first subtree, truncated to N − |C| nodes, is attached below C. One exact pass over the
W12 weights verifies the combined 32-node tree and accepts the longest matching path. TLV is
lossless because only the exact pass accepts tokens. Under TLV, τ denotes tokens per exact pass
and Tstep is the time of the two-pass cycle, including both drafting steps.
sections.content: Zero-copy pass. TLV does not maintain separate low-precision target model, since it reads the 8-bit view already nested in W12. This view is the first two thirds of each W12 record. With the dropped mantissa bits set to their midpoint, the pass matches the exact passs top-1 token at 98.7% of positions, whereas the exact pass reads the full records.

sections.title: 5 Evaluation
sections.content: We examine whether the speedups hold across drafters, targets, serving regimes and GPU platforms (5.2) and whether memory carries them to new deployments (5.3).

sections.title:
5.1 Setup
Hardware and agents. Each SGLang [23] server uses one H100 SXM5 or RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
Server Edition (sm 120, 1.51 TB/s measured), on a frozen v0.5.20 build, token-identical to the
release. Agents are Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code [15].
sections.content: Models and requests. With one request, all targets run in BF16: Qwen3.8-27B [14] with DFlash2 on both GPUs and with DSpark on H100, and Muse-Glimmer-30B [24] with DFlash2 on the RTX PRO 6000. With batching on H100, Qwen3.8-27B runs with DFlash2 or DSpark in FP8, and with DFlash2 in BF16 at 6, 8 and 10 requests as GPU memory allows. Qwen3.5-4B [25] uses DFlash2 and Gemma-4-12B [26] uses EAGLE-3, both in BF16. Requests are from GSM8K [27], HumanEval [28], MATH500 [29, 30], MBPP [31] and MT-Bench [32]. Decoding is greedy with thinking enabled, and batched clients run closed-loop with fixed number of requests in flight (the batch size). Metrics. gain is the geometric mean of per-request output-rate ratios per benchmark and batch size, combined by an equal-weight geometric mean. Every gain over stock comes from sealed final (3.2) with two paired runs. Every final system passed token forcing. Speedups over AR (Tables 1 and 2) come from interleaved runs of AR, stock and SpecPilot on development requests, within 2% to +6% of the sealed gains on unseen requests. Baselines. To keep the comparison fair, stock is tuned for each GPU and regime, using the pretrained drafter and the fastest upstream SGLang options we found. On H100, stock DFlash2 drafts its trained block size, as in the released configuration. On the RTX PRO 6000, the best stock for Qwen3.8-27B uses block 12 with Triton attention and is 9.9% faster than the H100 configuration. No EAGLE-3 configuration beats the default by more than 2.4%. sections.title:
5.2 Main Results
With one request, SpecPilot is more than twice as fast as stock in every setting (Table 3), most on
Qwen3.8-27B on the RTX PRO 6000. Over AR, it reaches 8.86–9.41× on H100 and 10.63–10.87×
on the RTX PRO 6000 (Table 1). On H100, it is also 1.84× faster than the DDTree baseline.
sections.content: With batching on FP8 Qwen3.8-27B, SpecPilot beats stock at every batch size, by 1.85 with DFlash2 and 1.94 with DSpark overall, raising the speedup over AR from about 2 to 3.90 and 3.93  (Table 2)  . In BF16, it is 1.71 faster, at 5.67 over AR against 3.20 for stock. Targets with weaker stock gain more, 2.39 on Qwen3.5-4B and 3.11 on Gemma-4-12B, where stock trails AR.

sections.title:
5.3 Generality Through Memory
Memory generalizes across drafters, target models and GPU platforms, even to EAGLE-3, a
sequential drafter. In each new deployment, the agents reused validated mechanisms and
adapted them to the new drafter, model or GPU.
sections.content: New drafters. DSpark reused the tree, W12 and TLV entries, which one promotion applied together with the new DSpark lattice (2.110). DSpark also added the INT6 copy for the pass. EAGLE-3 on Gemma-4-12B reimplemented two designs from memory, W12 on the MLP and prompt admission. Its own entries attach an n-gram chain to the EAGLE tree, select nodes by acceptance probabilities calibrated on recorded trees and add single-KV-head attention kernels. Its first round reached sealed 2.67, and promotions like calibrated selection and prompt admission raised the final speedup to 3.11. new GPU platform. The RTX PRO 6000 has 99 KB of shared memory per thread block and no wgmma. Porting the H100 tree and W12 entries, with W12 on mma.sync and tree verification on the Triton attention backend, alone gave sealed 1.92 over stock, most of the final gain. TLV with split-KV verify attention, which splits each requests KV sequence across thread blocks, and an INT6/INT8 Q-pass copy raised it to 2.44. This exceeds its 2.12 ceiling over stock, which assumes one draft per pass (3.1). new model family. Muse-Glimmer-30B, dense model without recurrent layers, reused memory except the GDN entries. Its first promotion applied the tree, W12, TLV and the INT6/INT8 11 Figure 8: Single-request Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash2 on H100 over three rounds. Filled points mark steps of the algorithms in 4.14.3. copy, with exact sliding-window attention in the 32-node tree. Kernel fusion with L2 prefetching then raised the final speedup to 2.21 on the RTX PRO 6000.

sections.title:
6.1 How the System Evolved over Three Rounds
The system went from stock’s 184 to 416 tokens/s in three rounds (Figure 8), and each round faced
a different bottleneck. The cost model re-measured the ceiling each round, so the master redi-
rected its parallel search to the factor holding the most speed instead of refining the previous gain.
sections.content: Round one: tokens. Stock verified one chain though extra rows were nearly free, and the τ factor led the ceiling. The round built best-first trees (4.2) and reached 270 tokens/s. Exact replay showed better tree on this lattice would add little, which moved the bottleneck from tokens to the step. Round two: weight bytes. Reading target weights took 80% of the step, so the bytes per weight became the largest lever. The master opened direction on lossless 12-bit format (4.1) and kept it through three promotions across two rounds. Its value came from the kernel as much as the format, since the W12 GEMM decodes weights in registers and beats cuBLAS at the few rows of verify pass (6.3). Round three: the unit of step. The W12 single-pass step, with one exact pass, ran about 25% above its byte floors, and trees were near their best on the lattice, so neither factor had much headroom. The remaining gain lay in an assumption of the ceiling, one exact pass per draft. TLV removed it by drafting twice per exact pass (4.3), which nearly doubled tokens per exact pass and took the system to 416 tokens/s. Single-agent baseline. We compare SpecPilot with single-agent loop that lacks the cost model, in the same setting. After three rounds, this baseline reached only 1.34 over stock, compared with 2.13 for SpecPilot. Without ceilings to rank the gaps, it focused on the most visible one, tokens per step, adding 24-node best-first tree, longer drafter block and cheaper drafter weights. It never addressed the target weight reads, although they took 80% of the step. In contrast, SpecPilot recomputed the ceiling every round and followed the largest factor as it shifted, from trees to weight bytes (W12) and then to the unit of step (TLV). 12 Figure 9: W12 beyond speculative decoding, on H100. (a) AR decoding speedup over BF16 weights in SGLang with one request. (b) Weight memory in BF16 and W12. (c) W12 GEMM speedup over cuBLAS on Qwen3.8-27B projections at 1 and 32 rows, with cold L2.

sections.title:
6.3 W12 as a General Lossless Weight Format
W12 is a lossless weight format useful beyond speculative decoding. Every dense model we
encoded, from six families, compresses to about 12 bits per weight (§4.1), a quarter fewer bytes
in every converted layer, without changing any output. Its GEMM speeds up any matrix product
bound by weight bytes, which includes the single row of AR decoding as well as the few rows
of a verify pass.
sections.content: In AR decoding on SGLang, without speculation, W12 alone gives 1.191.28 speedup on Muse-Glimmer-30B, Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-12B and Llama-3.1-8B with one request (Figure 9a), and 1.131.20 with 32 requests. It shrinks the weights by 1422% (Figure 9b), which grows the KV pool 2.0 on Qwen3.8-27B and 2.5 on Muse-Glimmer-30B, leaving room for more requests. The shipped W12 GEMM beats cuBLAS on every Qwen3.8-27B projection, by 1.191.47 at one row, as in AR decoding, and by 1.171.35 at 32 rows, as in verify pass (Figure 9c). The first W12 kernel took 0.800.89 of cuBLASs time at 32 rows. On the RTX PRO 6000, W12 is 1.181.68 faster on all 13 shapes at up to 32 rows. 128-byte swizzled activation layout allows 48-row tiles, so W12 GEMMs stay near their byte floor and flat across verify rows.

sections.title:
6.4 Tree Gains in Exact Replay
Exact replay reruns tree selection and verification on recorded lattices, so it isolates the tree from
timing noise (Figure 10). On the 8-position lattice, best-first trees raise τ from 4.25 (stock chain)
to 5.38 at 32 nodes. Drafting 16 positions lifts the curve to 5.85 at 32 nodes and 6.25 at 63. At 16

sections.title:
6.5 Why Mechanisms Depend on the Regime
Mechanisms that spend more verify work per exact pass help with one request, where the weight
stream hides that work, and hurt with batching, where it adds up. Wide trees, W12 and TLV
gained with one request on all three Qwen3.8-27B deployments. With batching, 24-node trees lost
14.9% on the FP8 target, and on BF16 Qwen3.8-27B a 24-position block lost 9.9% and TLV 13%.
TLV’s Q pass cuts bytes only in the attention and recurrent-layer projections. With the Q pass at
0.80–0.88 of a step, a cycle must accept nearly twice the tokens of a single-pass step to break even.
sections.content: Mechanisms that choose rows selectively gain with batching. With DSpark, the shared node budget accepted 614% more tokens than equal-size per-request trees, and per-request drafter blocks gave 1.040. Prompt rows are cheap only if compute idles in the weight stream, so admitting only waiting prompts gained 3.5% (unpaired) at 24 requests, while admitting every short prompt lost.

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Agents for systems. LLM program search improves code with automated evaluators, as in FunSearch [33], AlphaEvolve [17] and ADRS [18], after AlphaDev [34] and search-based compilers such as Ansor [35]. KernelBench [36] scores generated GPU kernels, and CUDA-L1 [37] optimizes them with reinforcement learning. Drafters and trees. Medusa [38], EAGLE [3, 9, 39], Lookahead [40] and self-speculative methods [41, 42] change drafting. Sequoia [8], EAGLE-2 [9], OPT-Tree [43], DDTree [10] and CaDDTree [44] shape trees for acceptance or throughput, and the concurrent PCTree [45] builds trees from DSparks Markov head. Our best-first trees score each edge given its parent, unlike DDTree, and verify more nodes than drafted positions. With batching, requests share one node budget. STree [46] and TreeWY [22] verify hybrid-target trees without per-node state, and we add commit that replays the accepted path. Hierarchical speculation. Staged speculative decoding [47], TriForce [48] and ML-SpecQD [49] place an intermediate model between the drafter and the target, and QSpec [50] and 14 Figure 10: Tokens per step τ in exact replay of single-request DFlash2 on Qwen3.8-27B, against the number of verified nodes N. Best-first trees run on lattices drafted with 8 and 16 positions. The gray line is stocks 8-position chain, and the oracle on the 16-position lattice reaches 8.2 tokens per step. QuantSpec [51] draft with low-precision version of the target. In these methods, the intermediate model serves as drafter. TLV instead uses low-precision target as an intermediate verifier. It checks the drafters full tree without accepting tokens, and one exact pass verifies its matching path plus second draft (4.3). Speculation with batching. TurboSpec [11] adapts to goodput, MagicDec [12] handles large batches, and D-cut [13] prunes drafts across requests, while our node budget at GEMM plateau takes the most probable nodes of all requests. Lossless weight compression. ZipNN [52] and DFloat11 [53] entropy-code weights to save memory but decode them before the GEMM, and DFloat11 runs 4.86.7 slower than cuBLAS on H100. ZipServ [54] and Unweight [55] fuse decoding into the GEMM but do not consistently beat cuBLAS on HBM GPUs. W12 gives every weight fixed 12-bit record that the GEMM decodes in registers. To our knowledge, it is the first lossless format whose GEMM beats cuBLAS on H100, by 1.171.47 from 1 to 32 rows.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: This work introduces SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop for algorithm discovery and systems optimization in lossless speculative decoding. Through ceiling-guided discovery, SpecPilot adapts to the distinct bottlenecks of complex serving regimes. We evaluate SpecPilot across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stocks 4.46 to 10.87 with one request, and from 1.94 to 3.93 with batching.

sections.title: D Cost of the Loop
sections.content: A round takes 720 hours and 2086 GPU-hours (Table A4). The thirteen completed rounds took 164 hours and 530 GPU-hours in total, created 486 code changes and promoted 54 of them. setting reached in two rounds splits its work between them, and the second round starts from the final system of the first round. W12 Details W12 encodes every dense checkpoint we tried, from six model families, at 12.01312.020 bits per weight (Table A2). Fewer than 1.3 104 of the weights fall outside their channels 16-binade window, so the escape list stays small. In AR decoding, W12 keeps its gain as the batch size grows, from 1.191.28 with one request to 1.131.20 with 32 (Figure A4a, Table A6). The freed memory goes to the KV cache, whose pool grows 2.03 on Qwen3.8-27B and 2.54 on Muse-Glimmer-30B. W12 is not tied to one serving engine. In Hugging Face Transformers with static cache and CUDA graphs, it decodes Llama-3.1-8B 1.12 faster with one request. The W12 GEMM beats cuBLAS on every Qwen3.8-27B projection from 1 to 32 rows (Figure A4b). The LM head, the largest matrix, gains most, 1.351.47. With warm L2, the speedups at up to 32 rows are 1.081.45. Kernel directions failed because the W12 GEMM is bound by decode and SM issue rate. Trees wider than 32 nodes cost more than the lattice returned: on the W12 system, each node above 32 costs about 0.17 ms per step, against value of about 0.063 ms. For the nested view, each eighth of its bytes removed cost about 0.01 of top-1 agreement, twice what the saved time bought back.
